# Review

## Summary

The note defines its central terms well. *Fidelity* and *authority* get explicit inline definitions. The three capture layers are defined in a list. "Mechanical derivation rule" is made concrete at once with substring match as the example. "Source-span locator" is clear from the surrounding sentences.

The main gap is in "Capture is layered because it is forced to be". The section claims layering is not a design choice and supports that by citing the linked note's notions of an *inherited* constraint and a *boundary-preserving rival*. The sentence uses those terms in their technical sense but does not gloss them. "Provider-contingent rather than inherited" later relies on the same distinction. So the reader has to follow the link to see why the section's conclusion holds.

"Ingest" is a smaller case: the reader can infer it from the adjacent "capture step".

# Review

## Summary

Five of the seven Relevant Notes entries are inflated: each repeats a link the body already uses inline with its relationship fully articulated, and each footer entry is a bare title with no relationship label or context phrase.

## Assessment

The gate does not flag a footer entry just because the body also links the same note. The problem here is that these five entries also fail its second question: they carry no relation such as extends or grounds, and no framing absent from the body. The body already explains each one precisely: the general rule this claim instantiates, the derivation-rule requirement it applies, the forced-constraint test it passes, the complementary authority claim, and the ADR that supplies the evidence. As written, the footer only duplicates those links.

Two entries are not inflated:

- `Structure inference needs capture at the decision surface` is absent from the body, and its context phrase ("decision rationale rather than quote fidelity") tells a reader how it differs from this note.
- `Collection prototypes` is absent from the body, and its phrase points to a concrete demonstration of the grounding-layer marker.

A fix is either to give each of the five entries a typed relationship and a phrase saying what the reader gains by following it from the footer, or to drop them and leave the inline links to do the navigation.

# Review

## Summary

The verbatim/paraphrase distinction is load-bearing, but the third layer, second-hand, is decorative with respect to the note's argument.

## Structures examined

**The three-layer capture taxonomy.** Verbatim versus paraphrase drives every later inference. Verbatim has a mechanical derivation rule (substring match) and paraphrase does not, which is why notation cannot raise fidelity. The same split is the "full layer" difference a position-only locator would erase, and it is what collapses in the lossless-capture boundary case. Those two categories cannot be reduced to one sentence without losing those inferences.

The second-hand category is never used after it is introduced. Deleting it leaves the notation argument, the corollary and the scope section unchanged. It also sits awkwardly in a list that the section says is forced by finite context and copyright: a second-hand passage reaches the KB through an intermediary, not through trimming, and it can be captured verbatim. It provides a useful citation rule (name the intermediary), but that rule is a separate point the argument does not need. Either drop it from the stratification and mention it as an orthogonal provenance dimension, or show where the fidelity-ceiling argument depends on it.

**"Non-increasing".** This is formal-looking notation that does real work. It names the monotonicity property from which "only re-capture raises fidelity" follows, and it supports the prediction that no downstream gate or locator can raise a passage's grade.

**Fidelity versus authority.** This two-term distinction is load-bearing. It resolves an apparent conflict with the linked authority note and gives the composition rule: capture sets a ceiling, and authority is earned beneath it.

# Review

## Summary

The note is mostly tight. The opening thesis, the fidelity/authority contrast, the three-layer list, the derivation-rule argument in "Why notation cannot repair it", the locator corollary, the practical-consequence paragraph and the evidence footer each do distinct work. Deleting any of them would weaken the argument or remove grounding.

The redundancy sits in the Scope section's first paragraph. That paragraph has one real job: to state the lossless-capture case and the locator boundary that follows from it. An announcing opener and a recap closer wrap that job and add nothing to it. Removing both leaves the boundary intact and shorter.

A non-obvious pass: "Notation can *express* the fidelity bound. It cannot move it." restates the section's conclusion. It still earns its place because it turns the derivation argument into a memorable stance that the corollary then builds on. The second Scope paragraph also passes. It repeats the ingest-time condition, but it converts that condition into an operational rule: promote load-bearing passages at capture time or re-mine the authoritative artifact.

## Summary

Most of the note's figurative wording has a function. The *spent* / *earned* pairing in the opening ("is spent at capture and never replenished" versus authority "earned by post-capture work") sharpens a real contrast between fidelity and authority that the paragraph goes on to use: "capture sets a ceiling" and "earn authority beneath it". *Ceiling* names an upper bound precisely. The *debt* language in the scope section ("the debt is fixed at ingest … repaid deliberately") maps onto the note's mechanism: an unpreserved verbatim layer is a deficit that only re-capture removes. Those figures are kept.

The failures cluster in the Scope section. There, two uses of *earns* ("earns its boundaries", "earns its keep") add a deservingness connotation that the note does not establish. They state ideas that literal wording states at least as clearly. Both are local, so the outcome is WARN, not FAIL.

# Review

The note's framework is the three-layer stratification of a captured source: verbatim, paraphrase and second-hand. Its grounding definition is the note's own framing. Layers arise because capture of a long source is forced to be lossy, and each layer fixes a ceiling on the fidelity a citation can assert.

Boundary cases tested:

- **Simplest instance — a short source captured losslessly.** The Scope section handles this: the layers collapse and the bound becomes vacuous. It maps cleanly.
- **Verbatim copy of a second-hand text.** It fails to map to one layer. The verbatim layer is defined by reproduction fidelity, and the second-hand layer by the source chain. A passage can satisfy both definitions, so the list is not a single ordered scale of fidelity grades. The forcing argument (context window and copyright) also does not produce the second-hand layer. This case falls outside the claimed coverage and is the WARN.
- **Between verbatim and paraphrase — an ellipsis-trimmed quote, a bracketed substitution or an OCR-damaged conversion.** These can be placed only with strain. The note's criteria do not settle whether they are degraded verbatim or paraphrase.
- **Adjacent concept — a translation.** A translation is neither the source's own words nor the snapshot's summary. It is closest to paraphrase, which is workable under the stated criteria, so no separate finding is raised.

The taxonomy is already short, so expanding it is not the obvious fix. Separating the source-chain axis from the capture-fidelity axis, or stating that second-hand is a qualifier applied on top of the other two layers, would resolve the main case without adding weight.

# Review

The note separates fidelity from authority well. It defines both terms, attributes the authority claim to the linked trace-memory note, and states how the two compose. That passage passes.

The material conflation is in the corollary. Earlier sections introduce layers as kinds of material in a snapshot: a verbatim block, a paraphrase summary and second-hand text. The corollary then treats "the layer" as a provenance grade that a locator encodes alongside position. These are an object (a region of the artifact) and a property (a grade of a passage), and the two readings give different conclusions about whether position-only locators are underspecified. The sentence "Two spans at the same file offset can differ … by a full layer" makes sense only under the property reading, but the example illustrating it uses the region reading.

The "instance of a general rule" passage is noted as INFO. Instance versus analogy affects what is inherited, but nothing in the central argument rests on that choice.

Claim inventory:

- **Fidelity is non-increasing and only re-capture raises it.** This is a derivation from the layer definitions and the lack of a mechanical rule for paraphrase. It is presented as derived, which is appropriate.

- **The locator corollary.** It is marked "It follows", so it is a derivation.
- **The evidence footer.** It reports an observation, then attaches it to claims it does not test.

The main problem is spread from the footer. The checker found false verbatim marks. On the linked ADR's account, they were mostly editorial alterations of genuine quotations. That observation supports "hand-asserted verbatim is unreliable" but is presented as evidence for "the layering" as well. The unlinked casebook evidence cannot be assessed from the page.

# Review

**Claimed scope.** Two scopes are in play. (1) Citations to lossy captures can assert no more fidelity than the capture preserved, and no downstream notation, locator or gate can raise it. (2) Per the description and the layering section, capture is necessarily layered for any LLM-consumer framework over real documents.

**Presented support.** Claim 1 is derived from the layer definitions and the derived-copy rule's mechanical-derivation precondition. Its exercised domain matches its claimed domain: wherever a passage lacks a mechanical rule back to its source, notation cannot supply one. The Scope section correctly withdraws the claim for lossless sources. Claim 1 passes.

Claim 2 is derived from two premises, a finite context window and copyright trims, plus an unreported rival search, and is backed by one corpus observation (ADR 046's casebook run). Those premises hold for long sources under reproduction restrictions and for designs that store only what one read can consume. The claim is phrased for all frameworks with an LLM consumer and real sources. The note neither argues why the premises reach freely licensed long sources or chunked full-text snapshots, nor marks that reach as conjecture. Because claim 2 appears in the description and frames the note, this is a WARN rather than INFO.

# Friction check: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Central claim (one sentence):** A citation's provenance fidelity is capped by the capture layer (verbatim, paraphrase or second-hand) that holds the cited passage, and only re-capture from the authoritative artifact, not downstream notation, can raise that cap.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The claim commits to one consistent thing if re-capture counts as a new ingest rather than a downstream operation. Under that reading, "fixed at ingest", "non-increasing downstream" and "only re-capture raises it" can coexist. Tension appears in the wording, not in the commitment: "permanently downgraded" and "decided before any note is written" sit beside a remedy that lets an author quote-mine the authoritative artifact later. The author should make the ingest/re-capture boundary explicit, but the claim does not split into incompatible parts.

## Thinnest joints

The opening of the "Capture is layered" section ranks thinnest. It asserts that the layering is inherited by citing a test whose own note says it cannot certify inheritance, and its forcing reasons do not reach the second-hand layer. The locator corollary ranks next. It is presented as following from the main claim, but it rests on an unspecified offset whose most natural reading, a snapshot offset, would already separate the layers. The "one chance" instance ranks third because the note's own remedy (re-capture) contradicts it, and the linked note's boundaries point the other way.

The notation-cannot-repair joint is stronger: its conclusion is plausible, but its stated mechanism conflicts with the shipped checker the note cites as evidence. The scope joint is the strongest of the five. Only its wording overreaches by ignoring how the second-hand layer arises.

The evidence paragraph (eighteen of eighty-seven `verbatim`-marked spans failed to match) shows that naive marking fails. It does not show that those failures came from paraphrase-layer passages, or that the layering is forced, so it supports only the weaker half of the note.

## For the human
Look first at "The layering is not a design choice": either supply the positive derivation that the linked rival test says it cannot provide, or weaken the claim to "undemoted", and say separately where the second-hand layer comes from.

# Critique: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Note:** kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md
**Central commitment:** A citation's fidelity is capped by the capture layer that holds the passage (verbatim, paraphrase or second-hand). The cap is fixed at ingest and never rises downstream. Notation cannot raise it; only re-capture can.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opponent is a provenance engineer from reproducible-research and records-management practice, such as an archivist or the designer of a citation checker that runs against PDFs. They accept the narrow mechanism: writing `verbatim` beside a paraphrase does not make it verbatim. They reject the claim built around it. The note identifies "the capture" with the LLM-facing markdown snapshot. It then treats that snapshot's lossiness as the ceiling on every citation. Those are two different artifacts:

1. **The forcing argument covers only the consumer view.** The context window is a limit on what the LLM reads. Mechanical verification of a quote does not run in the context window; a substring test over extracted PDF text costs nothing there. The note already names the authoritative artifact ("the sibling PDF"), and the KB keeps full external copies in private snapshots. A design can therefore keep layered excerpts for the reader and retain full text as the check's ground truth. That is a boundary-preserving rival in the sense of the linked rival-test note. That note also says that failing to find a rival "certifies nothing", so it cannot support "the layering is not a design choice" even if no rival had been found.

2. **The ceiling is not fixed at ingest.** While the authoritative artifact is retained, a citation can quote it directly with a page locator, and a checker can verify the quote. The note's answer is that this is "re-capture". But if every operation that raises fidelity is renamed re-capture, "only re-capture raises fidelity" becomes true by definition. The substantive claim is then that fidelity is bounded by the most faithful retained ground truth reachable from the citation. That is precondition 3 of the derived-copy rule, a recomputable regime. It is not the history note's regime, in which the record is gone after production. The analogy to "history has one chance to become checkable" fits only when the original is not retained (dead URLs, unretained PDFs, intermediaries). Those are the second-hand cases, not long sources in general.

3. **The corollary contradicts the rule it relies on.** Within one file, layer is a function of position. If the snapshot marks its layers, a layer field in the locator is a derived copy of recomputable truth. The derived-copy rule says to check such a copy or omit it, not to require it in every locator.

On this view the note has a true local mechanism: a marker cannot upgrade the stratum it points into. But it presents that as a temporal law ("fixed at ingest", "one chance") and an inherited constraint ("forced"), and neither generalization survives retention of the authoritative artifact.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- Section "Why notation cannot repair it" fully answers the narrow version: no mechanical derivation rule links paraphrase to source, so a marker cannot move the bound. The attack concedes this.
- The opening paragraph ("The only operation that raises fidelity is re-capture") and the history paragraph ("recoverable only by returning to the authoritative artifact and capturing again") recognize the retained-artifact route. They file it as re-capture without noticing that this weakens "fixed at ingest" and "non-increasing" from a temporal claim to a claim about which ground truth the citation points at.
- Section "Capture is layered because it is forced to be" does not consider separating the LLM-facing snapshot from the verification ground truth. It also reverses the one-way logic of the rival-test note it cites.
- Section "Scope" handles short sources, where layers collapse. It does not handle long sources whose full text is retained for mechanical checking, which is the case the attack targets.
- The corollary does not engage the redundancy objection.

## Constructive findings

- Restate the central bound relative to the retained ground truth: "a citation's fidelity is bounded by the most faithful retained artifact it can be checked against". Make "fixed at ingest" a special case that holds when the authoritative artifact is not retained.
- Limit "forced" to the LLM-facing snapshot. Then either state the boundary invariant that excludes keeping out-of-context full text for verification, or present that design as the rival it is. Do not cite the rival-test note as certifying inheritance.
- Keep the history-note link only for the unretained or second-hand case. Elsewhere, link the claim to the derived-copy rule's precondition 3.
- Rewrite the corollary as "the layer must be resolvable from the locator: either derived from a layer-marked snapshot or encoded and validated". Drop the impossible same-offset example.
- Update the notation paragraph for ADR 046: a paraphrase marked `verbatim` is now a checked false copy that fails validation. It no longer survives as a trusted unchecked copy.
- Describe the ADR 046 mismatches accurately (editorial quoting edits). Alternatively, add evidence that paraphrase-layer passages were marked verbatim, if such evidence exists in the casebook corpus.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- "the two move in opposite directions": fidelity is non-increasing and authority is earned upward. That is a ceiling with growth beneath it, as the note's next sentence says, not opposite motion. The phrase overstates the contrast.
- The second Open Question (fidelity versus usefulness) concedes that the bound constrains verification, not the citation's value to a reader. The title's "cannot assert more fidelity" is safe on that reading. The opening claim that a claim "can be no better grounded than the capture step left it" conflates grounding with fidelity, which the authority paragraph had just separated.

# Premise decomposition: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** A citation's fidelity is bounded by the capture layer (verbatim, paraphrase or second-hand) that holds the cited passage; no citation notation, locator or review gate can raise it, and only re-capture from the authoritative artifact can.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment rests on three groups of premises.

1. **Why the layers exist and where they occur.** The argument assumes long sources cannot be captured losslessly and that this layering is forced rather than chosen. These premises set the regime where the claim does work ("wherever the sources are long").
2. **Why the bound cannot be crossed.** The argument assumes paraphrase has no mechanical derivation rule, so the derived-copy rule turns a mislabeled paraphrase into a forbidden trusted copy. It also assumes that re-capture is a distinct operation separate from downstream citation work, and that fidelity is separate from authority.
3. **What follows and what supports it.** The argument assumes a position-only locator would conflate two passages from different layers. It cites the ADR 046 mismatch count as evidence, and it assumes without saying so that a citation's layer is visible to its consumer.

The core mechanism survives the counterexample hunt: there is no mechanical check from paraphrase to source, so notation cannot change a passage's layer. The weaknesses are in the parts around it. The claim that long sources force the layering confuses capture with context loading and treats publication limits as capture limits, and its citation of the rival test reverses that note's direction. The definition of re-capture is broad enough to make "fixed at ingest" nearly definitional, and it weakens the practical claim that quality is decided before any note is written. The cited evidence counts edited verbatim quotes, not paraphrase passages promoted by notation. All of these failures are local. Each one narrows the scope or corrects the support. None of them breaks the conditional bound.

## For the human

Look first at the premise that long sources force lossy capture. A full-text local snapshot defeats it, and it sets the regime the Scope section claims the note covers.

# Role in the KB: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

## Role
The note supplies two things to other KB files. The first is a premise: a citation's provenance grade is fixed at capture, and only re-capture raises it, because a non-verbatim passage has no mechanical derivation rule. The second is the verbatim / paraphrase / second-hand layering behind ADR 046's grounding-layer markers. One theory note argues from it, and the shipped ADR justifies its unchecked markers with it. Two source ingests cite it as a principle, one of them in a stronger or broader sense than the body states, and one tag head lists it.
Relied on: the title claim (capture bounds citation fidelity), the paraphrase layer's lack of a derivation rule, re-capture as the only remedy, and the three-layer vocabulary (ADR 046). Unused: the fidelity/authority distinction, the forced-constraint argument for layering (context window, copyright, provider filters, the boundary-preserving-rival link), the link to "history has one chance to become checkable", the locator corollary, the Scope section on lossless short sources, the Open Questions and the ADR 046 evidence paragraph.
